Let's introduce the new variable $u = x^3+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\dfrac 1 3 \textrm{d}u = x^2 \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{{x}^{3}+1}\cdot \,{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{{x}^{3}+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,-2\text{d}u=8{x}^{3}\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 8{x}^{3}{e}^{4-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{4-{x}^{4}}\cdot 8{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot (-2)\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-2{e}^{4-{x}^{4}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u={z}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=2z\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=z\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int z{e}^{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =\int {e}^{{z}^{2}}\cdot z\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{z}^{2}}}{2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=2{x}^{2}-x.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4x-1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=(4x-1)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4x-1){e}^{2{x}^{2}-x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{2{x}^{2}-x}\cdot (4x-1)\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{2{x}^{2}-x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=5-2{x}^{3}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=6{x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6{x}^{2}{e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}\cdot 6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-{e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{x}^{3}+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u=3{x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}{e}^{3{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{3{x}^{3}+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3{x}^{3}+1}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{2}{e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}\,\text{d}x & =2\int {e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int {e}^{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's introduce the new variable $u= 1-x^4.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{ \textrm{d}u}{ \textrm{d}x} = -4x^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^3 \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{4} \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int {x^3\,{3^{1-x^4}} }\, \textrm{d}x 
&=\int {{3^{1-x^4}}\cdot x^3 }\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt]
&=  \int {3^{u}} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \textrm{d}u\\[5pt]
                                                     &= -\dfrac{1}{4}\int {3^{u}}  \textrm{d}u\\[5pt]
                                                     &=  -\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{3^{u}}{\ln 3} + C\\[5pt]
                                                     &=   -\dfrac{3^{1-x^4}}{4\ln 3}+ C.
\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u = e^{2x}+1.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 2e^{2x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{1}{2}\, \textrm{d}u = e^{2x} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{e}^{2x}+1}\cdot {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{e}^{2x}+1|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2x}+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that $e^{2x} + 1 > 0$ for all $x.$

Let's introduce the new variable $u=-2x^2.$ Differentiating gives $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-4x \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad -4 \, \textrm{d}u=16x \, \textrm{d}x. $$ Next, we determine the new limits of integration:
$x$ $0$ $\sqrt {\ln 4}$
$u$ $0$ $-2\ln 4$
Therefore, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}16x{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\cdot 16x\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\cdot (-4\,\text{d}u) \\ & =-4{\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\ & =-4{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\ & =-4({e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{0}) \\ & =-4(\frac{1}{16}-1) \\ & =4\left(\frac{15}{16}\right) \\ & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned} $$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that we want to calculate $$
\displaystyle \int 2x e^{x^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Notice that if we let $u = x^2,$ then both $u$ and its derivative $u'=2x$ appear in the integrand:

$$
\int \underbrace{2x}_{u'} e^{\overbrace{x^2}^u}\,\textrm d x
$$

Integrals like this can always be solved using substitution.

Let $u=x^2.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d u = 2x\,\textrm d x.
$$

We now substitute our expressions into the integral and evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\underbrace{2x\,\text{d}x}_{\text{d}u} \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}+C \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the following definite integral: $$ \displaystyle{\int_{0}^{3} xe^{x^{2}}\, \textrm{d}x} $$ We'll use the change of variable method, which comprises three steps: **Step1:** Change of variable in the integrand. Let's introduce the new variable $u = x^2.$ Differentiating gives $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{ \textrm{d}x} = 2x \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u = x \, \textrm{d}x. $$ **Step 2:** Find the new limits of integration. We create a table below to change our limits of integration from $x$ to $u{:}$
$x$ $0$ $3$
$u$ $0$ $9$
**Step 3:** Evaluate the integral in the new variable $u.$ $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{9}{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{9}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{9} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{9}-{e}^{0}) \\ & =\frac{{e}^{9}-1}{2}.\end{aligned} $$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=5+4x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 4 \textrm d u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {3}^{5+4x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {3}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {3}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{3}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{3}^{5+4x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C\end{aligned}
$$
